        public Vector2 B;         public Segment(Vector2 a, Vector2 b) { A = a; B = b; }     }      // Vertex type for MIConvexHull     public class Site : IVertex     {         public double X { get; set; }         public double Y { get; set; }         public Site(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; }         public double[] Position => new[] { X, Y };     }      // Entry point     class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // boundary             var boundary = new Rect(0, 0, 800, 600);              // sample sites             var sites = new List<Site>             {                 new Site(100, 120),                 new Site(260, 60),                 new Site(340, 210),                 new Site(480, 150),                 new Site(640, 320),                 new Site(720, 420),                 new Site(200, 520)             };              // Build Voronoi edges clipped to boundary             var edges = BuildFortuneVoronoi(sites, boundary);              // Print edges             foreach (var s in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({s.A.X:0.0},{s.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({s.B.X:0.0},{s.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Build Voronoi edges using Delaunay triangulation duals and clip to boundary         public static List<Segment> BuildFortuneVoronoi(List<Site> sites, Rect boundary)         {             // 1) Compute Delaunay triangulation (via MIConvexHull)             var tri = DelaunayTriangulation<Site, DTCell>.Create(sites);              // 2) Map vertex to index for stable edge-keying             var idx = new Dictionary<Site, int>();             for (int i = 0; i < sites.Count; i++) idx[sites[i]] = i;              // 3) For each Delaunay edge, collect circumcenters of adjacent triangles             var edgeToCenters = new Dictionary<(int, int), List<Vector2>>();              foreach (var cell in tri.Cells)             {                 // skip degenerate cells                 if (cell.Vertices.Length != 3) continue;                  var A = cell.Vertices[0];                 var B = cell.Vertices[1];                 var C = cell.Vertices[2];                  var pA = new Vector2((float)A.X, (float)A.Y);                 var pB = new Vector2((float)B.X, (float)B.Y);                 var pC = new Vector2((float)C.X, (float)C.Y);                  var center = Circumcenter(pA, pB, pC);                  int iA = idx[A], iB = idx[B], iC = idx[C];                  AddEdgeCenter(edgeToCenters, (Math.Min(iA, iB), Math.Max(iA, iB)), center);                 AddEdgeCenter(edgeToCenters, (Math.Min(iB, iC), Math.Max(iB, iC)), center);                 AddEdgeCenter(edgeToCenters, (Math.Min(iC, iA), Math.Max(iC, iA)), center);             }              // 4) Create Voronoi edges by connecting centers of adjacent triangles.             var edges = new List<Segment>();              foreach (var kvp in edgeToCenters)             {                 var centers = kvp.Value;                 int i = kvp.Key.Item1;                 int j = kvp.Key.Item2;                  if (centers.Count >= 2)                 {                     // interior edge: connect the two triangle centers (take any two)                     for (int t = 0; t < centers.Count - 1; t++)                     {                         var p = centers[t];                         var q = centers[t + 1];                         // clip finite edge to boundary                         if (ClipSegmentToRect(p, q, boundary, out Vector2 a, out Vector2 b))                             edges.Add(new Segment(a, b));                     }                 }                 else if (centers.Count == 1)                 {                     // unbounded edge: extend from the center outward along the perpendicular to the Delaunay edge                     var A = sites[i];                     var B = sites[j];                     var edgeVec = new Vector2((float)(B.X - A.X), (float)(B.Y - A.Y));                     var normal = new Vector2(-edgeVec.Y, edgeVec.X); // one perpendicular                     var mid = new Vector2((float)(A.X + B.X) / 2, (float)(A.Y + B.Y) / 2);                     var center = centers[0];                     // orient outward away from triangle interior                     if (Vector2.Dot(center - mid, normal) > 0) normal = -normal;                      var dir = Vector2.Normalize(normal);                     if (RayIntersectsRect(center, dir, boundary, out Vector2 end))                         edges.Add(new Segment(center, end));                 }             }              return edges;         }          // circumcenter of triangle (2D)         static Vector2 Circumcenter(Vector2 a, Vector2 b, Vector2 c)         {             double d = 2 * (a.X * (b.Y - c.Y) + b.X * (c.Y - a.Y) + c.X * (a.Y - b.Y));             if (Math.Abs(d) < 1e-12) return new Vector2(0, 0);             double a2 = a.X * a.X + a.Y * a.Y;             double b2 = b.X * b.X + b.Y * b.Y;             double c2 = c.X * c.X + c.Y * c.Y;              float ux = (float)((a2 * (b.Y - c.Y) + b2 * (c.Y - a.Y) + c2 * (a.Y - b.Y)) / d);             float uy = (float)((a2 * (c.X - b.X) + b2 * (a.X - c.X) + c2 * (b.X - a.X)) / d);             return new Vector2(ux, uy);         }          static void AddEdgeCenter(Dictionary<(int, int), List<Vector2>> dict, (int, int) key, Vector2 center)         {             if (!dict.TryGetValue(key, out var list))             {                 list = new List<Vector2>();                 dict[key] = list;             }             list.Add(center);         }          // clip a finite segment to a rectangle         static bool ClipSegmentToRect(Vector2 p, Vector2 q, Rect r, out Vector2 a, out Vector2 b)         {             a = default; b = default;             const double EPS = 1e-9;             double x1 = p.X, y1 = p.Y;             double x2 = q.X, y2 = q.Y;             double dx = x2 - x1;             double dy = y2 - y1;             double t0 = 0.0, t1 = 1.0;              if (!ClipTest(-dx, x1 - r.MinX, ref t0, ref t1, EPS)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dx, r.MaxX - x1, ref t0, ref t1, EPS)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(-dy, y1 - r.MinY, ref t0, ref t1, EPS)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dy, r.MaxY - y1, ref t0, ref t1, EPS)) return false;              a = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t0 * dx), (float)(y1 + t0 * dy));             b = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t1 * dx), (float)(y1 + t1 * dy));             return true;              bool ClipTest(double p, double q, ref double t0_, ref double t1_, double eps)             {                 if (Math.Abs(p) < eps)                 {                     if (q < 0) return false;                 }                 else                 {                     double t = q / p;                     if (p < 0)                     {                         if (t > t1_) return false;                         if (t > t0_) t0_ = t;                     }                     else                     {                         if (t < t0_) return false;                         if (t < t1_) t1_ = t;                     }                 }                 return true;             }         }          // ray from origin along dir clipped to rectangle boundary         static bool RayIntersectsRect(Vector2 origin, Vector2 dir, Rect r, out Vector2 end)         {             end = default;             double x = origin.X, y = origin.Y;             double dx = dir.X, dy = dir.Y;             double tMin = 0.0;             double tMax = double.PositiveInfinity;              if (Math.Abs(dx) < 1e-9)             {                 if (x < r.MinX || x > r.MaxX) return false;             }             else             {                 double tx1 = (r.MinX - x) / dx;                 double tx2 = (r.MaxX - x) / dx;                 double t1 = Math.Min(tx1, tx2);                 double t2 = Math.Max(tx1, tx2);                 tMin = Math.Max(tMin, t1);                 tMax = Math.Min(tMax, t2);                 if (tMin > tMax) return false;             }              if (Math.Abs(dy) < 1e-9)             {                 if (y < r.MinY || y > r.MaxY) return false;             }             else             {                 double ty1 = (r.MinY - y) / dy;                 double ty2 = (r.MaxY - y) / dy;                 double t1 = Math.Min(ty1, ty2);                 double t2 = Math.Max(ty1, ty2);                 tMin = Math.Max(tMin, t1);                 tMax = Math.Min(tMax, t2);                 if (tMin > tMax) return false;             }              if (tMax < 0) return false;              // exit point on boundary             end = new Vector2((float)(x + tMax * dx), (float)(y + tMax * dy));             return true;         }          // Lightweight wrapper for MIConvexHull cell (placeholder)         // In actual code, use the proper DTCell type from MIConvexHull         public class DTCell : TriangulationCell<Site>         {         }     } }
2|36: Here's an alternative approach: compute the Voronoi cells directly by clipping a boundary polygon (rectangle) with half-planes defined by each site pair. This yields the Fortune-style Voronoi regions clipped to a boundary without needing a Delaunay library.  ```csharp using System; using System.Collections.Generic;  namespace VoronoiHalfPlaneClip {     struct Pt     {         public double X, Y;         public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; }     }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle (CCW)             var boundary = new List<Pt> {                 new Pt(0, 0),                 new Pt(800, 0),                 new Pt(800, 600),                 new Pt(0, 600)             };              // Sample sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120),                 new Pt(260, 60),                 new Pt(340, 210),                 new Pt(480, 150),                 new Pt(640, 320),                 new Pt(720, 420),                 new Pt(200, 520)             };              var cells = BuildVoronoiClipped(sites, boundary);              for (int i = 0; i < sites.Count; i++)             {                 var poly = cells[i];                 Console.WriteLine($"Site {i} at ({sites[i].X},{sites[i].Y}) has {poly.Count} vertices");                 for (int k = 0; k < poly.Count; k++)                 {                     var p = poly[k];                     var q = poly[(k + 1) % poly.Count];                     Console.WriteLine($"  Edge: ({p.X:0.0},{p.Y:0.0}) -> ({q.X:0.0},{q.Y:0.0})");                 }             }         }          // Build Voronoi cells by clipping the boundary with half-planes         // For each site A, clip against half-planes towards A from every other site B         static List<List<Pt>> BuildVoronoi clipped(List<Pt> sites, List<Pt> boundary)         {             var result = new List<List<Pt>>();             for (int i = 0; i < sites.Count; i++)             {                 var A = sites[i];                 // Start with the boundary polygon                 var poly = new List<Pt>(boundary);                  // Clip by half-planes for all other sites B                 for (int j = 0; j < sites.Count; j++)                 {                     if (j == i) continue;                     var B = sites[j];                     // Half-plane: (B - A) · P <= (|B|^2 - |A|^2)/2                     double dx = B.X - A.X;                     double dy = B.Y - A.Y;                     double c = (B.X * B.X + B.Y * B.Y - A.X * A.X - A.Y * A.Y) / 2.0;                     poly = ClipWithHalfPlane(poly, dx, dy, c);                     if (poly.Count == 0) break;                 }                  result.Add(poly);             }             return result;         }          // Clip a simple polygon with the half-plane ax + by <= c         static List<Pt> ClipWithHalfPlane(List<Pt> poly, double a, double b, double c)         {             var outPoly = new List<Pt>();             if (poly.Count == 0) return outPoly;              int m = poly.Count;             for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)             {                 var S = poly[i];                 var E = poly[(i + 1) % m];                 bool insideS = a * S.X + b * S.Y <= c + 1e-9;                 bool insideE = a * E.X + b * E.Y <= c + 1e-9;                  if (insideE)                 {                     if (!insideS)                     {                         var I = Intersect(S, E, a, b, c);                         if (I != null) outPoly.Add(I.Value);                     }                     outPoly.Add(E);                 }                 else if (insideS)                 {                     var I = Intersect(S, E, a, b, c);                     if (I != null) outPoly.Add(I.Value);                 }             }             return outPoly;         }          // Intersection of segment S->E with line a x + b y = c         static Pt? Intersect(Pt S, Pt E, double a, double b, double c)         {             double dx = E.X - S.X;             double dy = E.Y - S.Y;             double denom = a * dx + b * dy;             if (Math.Abs(denom) < 1e-12) return null;             double t = (c - a * S.X - b * S.Y) / denom;             return new Pt(S.X + t * dx, S.Y + t * dy);         }     } } ```  Notes: - This approach yields the Voronoi regions clipped to the given boundary by iteratively intersecting half-planes, one per site pair. - It does not rely on a Delaunay library and is robust for modest site counts. For very large numbers of sites, more optimized algorithms or libraries would be preferable.
3|36: Here's a third approach: implement Delaunay triangulation with Bowyer–Watson from scratch (no external libs), derive the Voronoi diagram from triangle circumcenters, and clip the finite edges to a boundary rectangle. This yields a Fortune-like Voronoi mesh without relying on a Delaunay library, and then you can clip to any axis-aligned rectangle.  ```csharp using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Numerics;  namespace Voronoi BowyerWatsonDemo {     // 2D point with an id (real sites have non-negative ids)     public struct Pt     {         public double X, Y;         public int Id;         public Pt(double x, double y, int id)         {             X = x; Y = y; Id = id;         }     }      // Triangle in the evolving Delaunay triangulation     public class Tri     {         public Pt A, B, C;         public bool IsReal; // true for triangles built from real sites         private Vector2? _centroid;         private double? _r2;          public Tri(Pt a, Pt b, Pt c, bool isReal)         {             A = a; B = b; C = c; IsReal = isReal;         }          // Circumcenter of triangle (static helper)         public static Vector2 Circumcenter(Pt a, Pt b, Pt c)         {             double d = 2 * (a.X * (b.Y - c.Y) + b.X * (c.Y - a.Y) + c.X * (a.Y - b.Y));             if (Math.Abs(d) < 1e-12) return new Vector2(0, 0); // degenerate             double a2 = a.X * a.X + a.Y * a.Y;             double b2 = b.X * b.X + b.Y * b.Y;             double c2 = c.X * c.X + c.Y * c.Y;             float ux = (float)((a2 * (b.Y - c.Y) + b2 * (c.Y - a.Y) + c2 * (a.Y - b.Y)) / d);             float uy = (float)((a2 * (c.X - b.X) + b2 * (a.X - c.X) + c2 * (b.X - a.X)) / d);             return new Vector2(ux, uy);         }          public Vector2 Center         {             get             {                 if (!_centroid.HasValue)                     _centroid = Circumcenter(A, B, C);                 return _centroid.Value;             }         }          public double Radius2         {             get             {                 if (!_r2.HasValue)                 {                     var c = Center;                     double dx = A.X - c.X, dy = A.Y - c.Y;                     _r2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;                 }                 return _r2.Value;             }         }          // Check if point p lies inside the circumcircle         public bool ContainsInCircumcircle(Pt p)         {             var c = Center;             double dx = p.X - c.X, dy = p.Y - c.Y;             double d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;             return d2 <= Radius2 + 1e-9;         }     }      // Edge key for adjacency (order-independent)     struct EdgeKey : IEquatable<EdgeKey>     {         public int A, B;         public EdgeKey(int a, int b)         {             if (a < b) { A = a; B = b; }             else { A = b; B = a; }         }         public bool Equals(EdgeKey other) => A == other.A && B == other.B;         public override bool Equals(object obj) => obj is EdgeKey k && Equals(k);         public override int GetHashCode() => A.GetHashCode() ^ B.GetHashCode();     }      // Boundary clipping rectangle     public struct Rect     {         public double MinX, MinY, MaxX, MaxY;         public Rect(double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)         {             MinX = minX; MinY = minY; MaxX = maxX; MaxY = maxY;         }     }      // Voronoi edge segment     public struct Segment     {         public Vector2 A, B;         public Segment(Vector2 a, Vector2 b) { A = a; B = b; }     }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             var boundary = new Rect(0, 0, 800, 600);              // Real sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120, 0),                 new Pt(260, 60, 1),                 new Pt(340, 210, 2),                 new Pt(480, 150, 3),                 new Pt(640, 320, 4),                 new Pt(720, 420, 5),                 new Pt(200, 520, 6)             };              // Compute Voronoi via Bowyer–Watson + circumcenters, then clip edges             var edges = BowyerWatsonVoronoiClipped(sites, boundary);              foreach (var s in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({s.A.X:0.0},{s.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({s.B.X:0.0},{s.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Bowyer–Watson Delaunay triangulation + Voronoi edge extraction + boundary clipping         public static List<Segment> BowyerWatsonVoronoiClipped(List<Pt> sites, Rect boundary)         {             // 1) Create a large super-triangle that contains all sites             double minX = double.MaxValue, minY = double.MaxValue, maxX = double.MinValue, maxY = double.MinValue;             foreach (var p in sites)             {                 if (p.X < minX) minX = p.X;                 if (p.Y < minY) minY = p.Y;                 if (p.X > maxX) maxX = p.X;                 if (p.Y > maxY) maxY = p.Y;             }             double dx = maxX - minX;             double dy = maxY - minY;             double delta = Math.Max(dx, dy) * 10.0 + 1.0;              var pS1 = new Pt(minX - delta, minY - delta, -1);             var pS2 = new Pt(minX - delta, maxY + delta, -2);             var pS3 = new Pt(maxX + delta, minY - delta, -3);              var triangulation = new List<Tri>();             triangulation.Add(new Tri(pS1, pS2, pS3, false)); // entirely fake              // 2) Bowyer–Watson insertion of real sites             foreach (var p in sites)             {                 var bad = new List<Tri>();                 foreach (var t in triangulation)                 {                     if (t.ContainsInCircumcircle(p))                         bad.Add(t);                 }                 if (bad.Count == 0) continue;                  // Boundary edges of the polygonal hole                 var edgeCount = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, int>();                 var edgeVerts = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, (Pt A, Pt B)>();                  foreach (var t in bad)                 {                     TryAddEdge(t.A, t.B, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                     TryAddEdge(t.B, t.C, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                     TryAddEdge(t.C, t.A, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                 }                  // Edges that appear only once are boundary edges                 var boundaryEdges = new List<(Pt A, Pt B)>();                 foreach (var kv in edgeCount)                 {                     if (kv.Value == 1)                         boundaryEdges.Add(edgeVerts[kv.Key]);                 }                  // Remove bad triangles                 foreach (var t in bad) triangulation.Remove(t);                  // Re-triangulate the hole by connecting new point to boundary edges                 foreach (var eb in boundaryEdges)                 {                     triangulation.Add(new Tri(p, eb.A, eb.B, true));                 }             }              // 3) Remove any triangles that use super-triangle vertices             triangulation.RemoveAll(t => t.A.Id < 0 || t.B.Id < 0 || t.C.Id < 0);              // 4) Build Voronoi edges: connect circumcenters of adjacent triangles             // Map edge -> list of adjacent triangle centers             var edgeToCenters = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, List<Vector2>>();             foreach (var t in triangulation)             {                 var center = Tri.Circumcenter(t.A, t.B, t.C);                 // For each triangle edge, associate its circumcenter                 AddCenterEdge(t.A, t.B, center, edgeToCenters);                 AddCenterEdge(t.B, t.C, center, edgeToCenters);                 AddCenterEdge(t.C, t.A, center, edgeToCenters);             }              // 5) Build finite Voronoi edges (only edges with >=2 neighboring triangles)             var voronoiEdges = new List<Segment>();             foreach (var kv in edgeToCenters)             {                 var centers = kv.Value;                 if (centers.Count >= 2)                 {                     // If more than two centers share an edge (degenerate), connect sequentially                     for (int i = 0; i < centers.Count - 1; i++)                     {                         var a = centers[i];                         var b = centers[i + 1];                         if (ClipSegmentToRect(a, b, boundary, out Vector2 A, out Vector2 B))                             voronoiEdges.Add(new Segment(A, B));                     }                 }             }              return voronoiEdges;         }          // Helper: add an edge's boundary center to the map         static void AddCenterEdge(Pt a, Pt b, Vector2 center, Dictionary<EdgeKey, List<Vector2>> map)         {             var k = new EdgeKey(a.Id, b.Id);             if (!map.TryGetValue(k, out var list))             {                 list = new List<Vector2>();                 map[k] = list;             }             list.Add(center);         }          // Try to insert an edge into the boundary edge map         static void TryAddEdge(Pt a, Pt b, List<Tri> bad,             Dictionary<EdgeKey, int> edgeCount,             Dictionary<EdgeKey, (Pt A, Pt B)> edgeVerts)         {             var k = new EdgeKey(a.Id, b.Id);             if (!edgeCount.ContainsKey(k)) edgeCount[k] = 0;             edgeCount[k]++;              // Store endpoints (one time is enough)             if (!edgeVerts.ContainsKey(k))                 edgeVerts[k] = (a, b);         }          // Clip a segment to a rectangle (Cohen-Sutherland style like)         static bool ClipSegmentToRect(Vector2 p, Vector2 q, Rect r, out Vector2 a, out Vector2 b)         {             a = default; b = default;             double x1 = p.X, y1 = p.Y;             double x2 = q.X, y2 = q.Y;             double dx = x2 - x1;             double dy = y2 - y1;             double t0 = 0.0, t1 = 1.0;             const double EPS = 1e-12;              bool ClipTest(double p_, double q_, ref double t0_, ref double t1_)             {                 if (Math.Abs(p_) < EPS)                 {                     if (q_ < 0) return false;                 }                 else                 {                     double t = q_ / p_;                     if (p_ < 0)                     {                         if (t > t1_) return false;                         if (t > t0_) t0_ = t;                     }                     else                     {                         if (t < t0_) return false;                         if (t < t1_) t1_ = t;                     }                 }                 return true;             }              if (!ClipTest(-dx, x1 - r.MinX, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dx, r.MaxX - x1, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(-dy, y1 - r.MinY, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dy, r.MaxY - y1, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;              a = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t0 * dx), (float)(y1 + t0 * dy));             b = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t1 * dx), (float)(y1 + t1 * dy));             return true;         }     } } ```  Notes: - This approach builds a Delaunay triangulation from scratch using Bowyer–Watson, then turns triangle circumcenters into Voronoi vertices and connects centers for adjacent triangles to form finite Voronoi edges. - Edges that would be unbounded in an infinite diagram are dropped (by filtering after removing super-triangle triangles). Finite edges are then clipped to the given boundary rectangle. - No external libraries are required; it’s self-contained and suitable for learning or small-scale use. For very large point sets, using a dedicated library or a more optimized implementation is recommended.
4|36: // Another approach: Bowyer–Watson Delaunay triangulation (from scratch) + Voronoi dual, // then clip Voronoi edges to a rectangular boundary. No external libraries required. // This is self-contained and yields a Fortune-like Voronoi mesh.  using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Numerics;  namespace VoronoiBowyerWatsonDemo {     // 2D point with an id     public struct Pt     {         public double X, Y;         public int Id;         public Pt(double x, double y, int id)         {             X = x; Y = y; Id = id;         }     }      // Triangle in Delaunay triangulation     public class Tri     {         public Pt A, B, C;         public bool Real; // true for triangles formed from real sites          private Vector2? _circumCenter;         private double? _circumR2;          public Tri(Pt a, Pt b, Pt c, bool real)         {             A = a; B = b; C = c; Real = real;         }          // Circumcenter of triangle         public Vector2 CircumCenter         {             get             {                 if (!_circumCenter.HasValue)                     _circumCenter = ComputeCircumcenter(A, B, C);                 return _circumCenter.Value;             }         }          // Radius^2 of circumcircle         public double circumR2         {             get             {                 if (!_circumR2.HasValue)                 {                     var cc = CircumCenter;                     double dx = A.X - cc.X;                     double dy = A.Y - cc.Y;                     _circumR2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;                 }                 return _circumR2.Value;             }         }          // Whether point p lies inside the circumcircle         public bool ContainsInCircumcircle(Pt p)         {             var cc = CircumCenter;             double dx = p.X - cc.X;             double dy = p.Y - cc.Y;             double d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;             return d2 <= circumR2 + 1e-9;         }          // Static circumcenter helper         static Vector2 ComputeCircumcenter(Pt a, Pt b, Pt c)         {             double d = 2 * (a.X * (b.Y - c.Y) + b.X * (c.Y - a.Y) + c.X * (a.Y - b.Y));             if (Math.Abs(d) < 1e-12) return new Vector2(0, 0);             double a2 = a.X * a.X + a.Y * a.Y;             double b2 = b.X * b.X + b.Y * b.Y;             double c2 = c.X * c.X + c.Y * c.Y;             float ux = (float)((a2 * (b.Y - c.Y) + b2 * (c.Y - a.Y) + c2 * (a.Y - b.Y)) / d);             float uy = (float)((a2 * (c.X - b.X) + b2 * (a.X - c.X) + c2 * (b.X - a.X)) / d);             return new Vector2(ux, uy);         }     }      // Simple pair key for an undirected edge (order-independent)     struct EdgeKey : IEquatable<EdgeKey>     {         public int A, B;         public EdgeKey(int a, int b)         {             if (a < b) { A = a; B = b; }             else { A = b; B = a; }         }         public bool Equals(EdgeKey other) => A == other.A && B == other.B;         public override bool Equals(object obj) => obj is EdgeKey k && Equals(k);         public override int GetHashCode() => A.GetHashCode() ^ B.GetHashCode();     }      // Boundary rectangle     public struct Rect     {         public double MinX, MinY, MaxX, MaxY;         public Rect(double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)         {             MinX = minX; MinY = minY; MaxX = maxX; MaxY = maxY;         }     }      // Voronoi edge segment     public struct Segment     {         public Vector2 A, B;         public Segment(Vector2 a, Vector2 b) { A = a; B = b; }     }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             var boundary = new Rect(0, 0, 800, 600);              // Real sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120, 0),                 new Pt(260, 60, 1),                 new Pt(340, 210, 2),                 new Pt(480, 150, 3),                 new Pt(640, 320, 4),                 new Pt(720, 420, 5),                 new Pt(200, 520, 6)             };              // Compute Voronoi via Bowyer–Watson + clip to boundary             var edges = BowyerWatsonVoronoiClipped(sites, boundary);              foreach (var s in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({s.A.X:0.0},{s.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({s.B.X:0.0},{s.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Bowyer–Watson Delaunay triangulation + Voronoi edges + boundary clipping         public static List<Segment> BowyerWatsonVoronoiClipped(List<Pt> sites, Rect boundary)         {             // 1) Create a large super-triangle that contains all sites             double minX = double.MaxValue, minY = double.MaxValue, maxX = double.MinValue, maxY = double.MinValue;             foreach (var p in sites)             {                 if (p.X < minX) minX = p.X;                 if (p.Y < minY) minY = p.Y;                 if (p.X > maxX) maxX = p.X;                 if (p.Y > maxY) maxY = p.Y;             }             double dx = maxX - minX;             double dy = maxY - minY;             double delta = Math.Max(dx, dy) * 10.0 + 1.0;              var pS1 = new Pt(minX - delta, minY - delta, -1);             var pS2 = new Pt(minX - delta, maxY + delta, -2);             var pS3 = new Pt(maxX + delta, minY - delta, -3);              var triangulation = new List<Tri>();             triangulation.Add(new Tri(pS1, pS2, pS3, false)); // super-triangle              // 2) Bowyer–Watson insertion of real sites             foreach (var p in sites)             {                 var bad = new List<Tri>();                 foreach (var t in triangulation)                 {                     if (t.ContainsInCircumcircle(p))                         bad.Add(t);                 }                 if (bad.Count == 0) continue;                  // Collect boundary edges of the hole                 var edgeCount = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, int>();                 var edgeVerts = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, (Pt A, Pt B)>();                  foreach (var t in bad)                 {                     AddEdge(t.A, t.B, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                     AddEdge(t.B, t.C, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                     AddEdge(t.C, t.A, bad, edgeCount, edgeVerts);                 }                  // Boundary edges (appear once)                 var boundaryEdges = new List<(Pt A, Pt B)>();                 foreach (var kv in edgeCount)                 {                     if (kv.Value == 1)                         boundaryEdges.Add(edgeVerts[kv.Key]);                 }                  // Remove bad triangles                 foreach (var t in bad) triangulation.Remove(t);                  // Re-triangulate hole with new point                 foreach (var eb in boundaryEdges)                 {                     triangulation.Add(new Tri(p, eb.A, eb.B, true));                 }             }              // 3) Remove triangles that use super-triangle vertices             triangulation.RemoveAll(t => t.A.Id < 0 || t.B.Id < 0 || t.C.Id < 0);              // 4) Build Voronoi edges: connect circumcenters of adjacent triangles             var edgeToCenters = new Dictionary<EdgeKey, List<Vector2>>();             foreach (var t in triangulation)             {                 var center = t.CircumCenter;                 AddCenterEdge(t.A, t.B, center, edgeToCenters);                 AddCenterEdge(t.B, t.C, center, edgeToCenters);                 AddCenterEdge(t.C, t.A, center, edgeToCenters);             }              // 5) Build finite Voronoi edges (edges with >= 2 neighboring triangles)             var voronoiEdges = new List<Segment>();             foreach (var kv in edgeToCenters)             {                 var centers = kv.Value;                 if (centers.Count >= 2)                 {                     // Connect centers pairwise                     for (int i = 0; i < centers.Count - 1; i++)                     {                         var a = centers[i];                         var b = centers[i + 1];                         if (ClipSegmentToRect(a, b, boundary, out Vector2 A, out Vector2 B))                             voronoiEdges.Add(new Segment(A, B));                     }                 }             }              return voronoiEdges;         }          // Helpers          static void AddEdge(Pt a, Pt b, List<Tri> bad,             Dictionary<EdgeKey, int> edgeCount,             Dictionary<EdgeKey, (Pt A, Pt B)> edgeVerts)         {             var k = new EdgeKey(a.Id, b.Id);             if (!edgeCount.ContainsKey(k)) edgeCount[k] = 0;             edgeCount[k]++;              if (!edgeVerts.ContainsKey(k))                 edgeVerts[k] = (a, b);         }          static void AddCenterEdge(Pt a, Pt b, Vector2 center, Dictionary<EdgeKey, List<Vector2>> map)         {             var key = new EdgeKey(a.Id, b.Id);             if (!map.TryGetValue(key, out var list))             {                 list = new List<Vector2>();                 map[key] = list;             }             list.Add(center);         }          // Clip a segment to a rectangle (Cohen–Sutherland-like)         static bool ClipSegmentToRect(Vector2 p, Vector2 q, Rect r, out Vector2 a, out Vector2 b)         {             a = default; b = default;             double x1 = p.X, y1 = p.Y;             double x2 = q.X, y2 = q.Y;             double dx = x2 - x1;             double dy = y2 - y1;             double t0 = 0.0, t1 = 1.0;             const double EPS = 1e-12;              bool ClipTest(double p_, double q_, ref double t0_, ref double t1_)             {                 if (Math.Abs(p_) < EPS)                 {                     if (q_ < 0) return false;                 }                 else                 {                     double t = q_ / p_;                     if (p_ < 0)                     {                         if (t > t1_) return false;                         if (t > t0_) t0_ = t;                     }                     else                     {                         if (t < t0_) return false;                         if (t < t1_) t1_ = t;                     }                 }                 return true;             }              if (!ClipTest(-dx, x1 - r.MinX, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dx, r.MaxX - x1, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(-dy, y1 - r.MinY, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;             if (!ClipTest(dy, r.MaxY - y1, ref t0, ref t1)) return false;              a = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t0 * dx), (float)(y1 + t0 * dy));             b = new Vector2((float)(x1 + t1 * dx), (float)(y1 + t1 * dy));             return true;         }          // Circumcenter + helper         // (Defined inside Tri class; used there)          // End helpers     } }
5|36: Here's a different approach: use NetTopologySuite's VoronoiDiagramBuilder to generate the Voronoi diagram and clip it directly to a boundary rectangle. 6|36: Here's a different approach: compute each Voronoi cell by clipping the boundary with half-planes corresponding to every other site, but implement the clipping using the Clipper library (polygon clipping) to avoid manual Sutherland–Hodgman code. This yields exact cells (Fortune-style) clipped to a rectangle without requiring a Delaunay library.  ```csharp // 2D Fortune-like Voronoi clipped to a boundary using per-site half-planes with Clipper // Requires: ClipierLib (Clipper library) via NuGet: ClipTool or ClippeLib (ClipperLib)  using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using ClipperLib;  namespace VoronoiHalfPlaneClipper {     // simple double-precision point     struct Pt { public double X, Y; public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; } }      // Voronoi edge segment     struct Segment { public Pt A, B; public Segment(Pt a, Pt b) { A = a; B = b; } }      class Program     {         // scale for int-point conversion (Clipper uses integers)         const double Scale = 1000.0;          static void Main()         {             // boundary rectangle (CCW)             var boundary = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(0, 0),                 new Pt(800, 0),                 new Pt(800, 600),                 new Pt(0, 600)             };              // sample sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120),                 new Pt(260, 60),                 new Pt(340, 210),                 new Pt(480, 150),                 new Pt(640, 320),                 new Pt(720, 420),                 new Pt(200, 520)             };              var edges = BuildVoronoiClipped(sites, boundary);              foreach (var s in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({s.A.X:0.0},{s.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({s.B.X:0.0},{s.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Build Voronoi edges by clipping the boundary with half-planes: closer to site i than site j         public static List<Segment> BuildVoronoiClipped(List<Pt> sites, List<Pt> boundary)         {             // convert boundary to int path for Clipper             var boundaryPath = ToIntPath(boundary);              var allEdges = new List<Segment>();              for (int i = 0; i < sites.Count; i++)             {                 var A = sites[i];                 // current cell initial polygon is the boundary                 var current = new List<List<IntPoint>> { boundaryPath };                  // clip against half-planes (A closer than every other site B)                 for (int j = 0; j < sites.Count; j++)                 {                     if (j == i) continue;                     var B = sites[j];                      // half-plane: a x + b y <= c, where:                     // a = (Bx - Ax), b = (By - Ay), c = (Bx^2 + By^2 - Ax^2 - Ay^2)/2                     double a = B.X - A.X;                     double b = B.Y - A.Y;                     double c = (B.X * B.X + B.Y * B.Y - A.X * A.X - A.Y * A.Y) / 2.0;                      // construct a polygon that represents the half-plane a x + b y <= c                     var hp = HalfPlanePolygon(a, b, c);                      // clip every current polygon by this half-plane polygon                     var next = new List<List<IntPoint>>();                     foreach (var poly in current)                     {                         var clipper = new Clipper();                         clipper.AddPath(poly, PolyType.ptSubject, true);                         clipper.AddPath(hp, PolyType.ptClip, true);                         var solution = new List<List<IntPoint>>();                         clipper.Execute(ClipType.Intersection, solution, PolyFillType.pftNonZero, PolyFillType.pftNonZero);                         foreach (var sPath in solution)                             next.Add(sPath);                     }                     current = next;                     // if nothing left, break early                     if (current.Count == 0) break;                 }                  // collect edges from resulting polygons for this site                 foreach (var poly in current)                 {                     int m = poly.Count;                     for (int k = 0; k < m; k++)                     {                         var p = poly[k];                         var q = poly[(k + 1) % m];                         var Aout = FromIntPoint(p);                         var Bout = FromIntPoint(q);                         allEdges.Add(new Segment(Aout, Bout));                     }                 }             }              return allEdges;         }          // Construct a polygon approximating the half-plane a x + b y <= c         // Strategy: create a large parallelogram along the line a x + b y = c,         // and extend far on the inner side of the half-plane (towards the normal n=(a,b)).         static List<IntPoint> HalfPlanePolygon(double a, double b, double c)         {             // pick a point on the line             double px, py;             if (Math.Abs(a) > Math.Abs(b))             {                 px = c / a; py = 0;             }             else             {                 px = 0; py = c / b;             }              // line direction vector along the line: d = (-b, a)             double dx = -b, dy = a;             double len = Math.Sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);             if (len < 1e-12) {                 // degenerate; fall back to a large rectangle far away                 dx = 1; dy = 0; len = 1;             }             // normalize direction             dx /= len; dy /= len;              // a large distance to extend along the line             double L = 1e6;              // two points on the line far apart             double x1 = px - dx * L, y1 = py - dy * L;             double x2 = px + dx * L, y2 = py + dy * L;              // normal vector pointing towards the half-plane a x + b y <= c             // check which side p1 lies on             bool p1Inside = (a * x1 + b * y1 <= c + 1e-9);              // extend far in the inside direction along the normal             double nx = a, ny = b;             double nlen = Math.Sqrt(nx * nx + ny * ny);             if (nlen > 0) { nx /= nlen; ny /= nlen; }              double ext = 1e6;             double x3, y3, x4, y4;             if (p1Inside)             {                 x3 = x2 + nx * ext; y3 = y2 + ny * ext;                 x4 = x1 + nx * ext; y4 = y1 + ny * ext;             }             else             {                 // take the opposite side                 x3 = x2 - nx * ext; y3 = y2 - ny * ext;                 x4 = x1 - nx * ext; y4 = y1 - ny * ext;             }              // polygon order (CCW)             var hp = new List<IntPoint>             {                 ToIntPoint(x1, y1),                 ToIntPoint(x2, y2),                 ToIntPoint(x3, y3),                 ToIntPoint(x4, y4)             };             return hp;         }          // helpers: convert between Pt and Clippoint         static IntPoint ToIntPoint(double x, double y)             => new IntPoint((long)(x * Scale), (long)(y * Scale));          static IntPoint ToIntPoint(Pt p) => ToIntPoint(p.X, p.Y);          static Pt FromIntPoint(IntPoint p) => new Pt(p.X / Scale, p.Y / Scale);          static List<IntPoint> ToIntPath(List<Pt> poly)         {             var path = new List<IntPoint>(poly.Count);             foreach (var p in poly) path.Add(ToIntPoint(p));             return path;         }          static Pt FromPt(Pt p) => p;          // convenience: convert         static Pt FromIntPoint(IntPoint p) => new Pt(p.X / Scale, p.Y / Scale);     } } ```  Notes: - This method clips the boundary polygon against a half-plane for every other site, effectively constructing each Voronoi cell as the intersection of the boundary with all relevant half-planes. - It uses Clipper for robust polygon clipping and a custom half-plane polygon generator to represent each half-plane as a large convex polygon. - The resulting edges are finite segments clipped to the boundary. As with any clipping-based method, numerical robustness depends on the scale and the clipping tolerance; the 1e-9 tol in the inside-test helps.
7|36: Here is a self-contained alternative: compute the Voronoi edges by intersecting the perpendicular bisector of every site pair with the intersection of all half-planes that keep points closer to the two sites than to any other site, then clip to a rectangle. This avoids Delaunay libraries and yields exact edges clipped to a boundary.  ```csharp using System; using System.Collections.Generic;  namespace VoronoiBisectorClipped {     struct Pt { public double X, Y; public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; } }      struct Seg { public Pt A, B; public Seg(Pt a, Pt b) { A = a; B = b; } }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             double minX = 0, minY = 0, maxX = 800, maxY = 600;              // Sample sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120),                 new Pt(260, 60),                 new Pt(340, 210),                 new Pt(480, 150),                 new Pt(640, 320),                 new Pt(720, 420),                 new Pt(200, 520)             };              var edges = BuildVoronoiEdgesBisector(sites, minX, minY, maxX, maxY);              foreach (var e in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({e.A.X:0.0},{e.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({e.B.X:0.0},{e.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Build edges by intersecting each pair's perpendicular bisector with all site-half-planes and the boundary         static List<Seg> BuildVoronoiEdgesBisector(List<Pt> sites, double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)         {             var edges = new List<Seg>();             int n = sites.Count;             const double EPS = 1e-12;              for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)             {                 for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)                 {                     // Perpendicular bisector L: a x + b y = c                     var si = sites[i], sj = sites[j];                     double a = sj.X - si.X;                     double b = sj.Y - si.Y;                     double c = (sj.X * sj.X + sj.Y * sj.Y - si.X * si.X - si.Y * si.Y) / 2.0;                      // Pick a point p0 on L                     double p0x, p0y;                     if (Math.Abs(a) > Math.Abs(b) && Math.Abs(a) > EPS)                     {                         p0x = c / a;                         p0y = 0;                     }                     else if (Math.Abs(b) > EPS)                     {                         p0x = 0;                         p0y = c / b;                     }                     else                     {                         // Degenerate (shouldn't happen for distinct sites)                         continue;                     }                      // Direction along L: d = (-b, a)                     double dx = -b, dy = a;                      // t-parametrization: P(t) = p0 + t*(dx, dy)                     // Constraints: for all k != i, dist(P, si) <= dist(P, sk)                     // and clip to rectangle [minX,maxX] x [minY,maxY]                     double t0 = -1e100, t1 = 1e100;                      // Half-plane constraints: (sk - si)·P <= (|sk|^2 - |si|^2)/2                     for (int k = 0; k < n; k++)                     {                         if (k == i) continue;                         var sk = sites[k];                         double Ak = 2.0 * (sk.X - si.X);                         double Bk = 2.0 * (sk.Y - si.Y);                         double Ck = sk.X * sk.X + sk.Y * sk.Y - si.X * si.X - si.Y * si.Y;                          // Replace P by p0 + t*d                         double bound = Ck - (Ak * p0x + Bk * p0y);                         double coef = Ak * dx + Bk * dy; // coefficient of t                          if (Math.Abs(coef) < EPS)                         {                             // If coef ~ 0, inequality doesn't constrain t                             if (bound < -1e-9)                             {                                 // No solution                                 t0 = 1; t1 = 0; // empty                                 break;                             }                             continue;                         }                          double tBound = bound / coef;                         if (coef > 0)                         {                             // t <= tBound                             if (tBound < t1) t1 = tBound;                         }                         else                         {                             // coef < 0: t >= tBound                             if (tBound > t0) t0 = tBound;                         }                          if (t0 > t1) break; // empty                     }                      // Boundary clipping                     // x >= minX                     ClipAlongDx(ref t0, ref t1, dx, p0x, minX, true);                     // x <= maxX                     ClipAlongDx(ref t0, ref t1, dx, p0x, maxX, false);                     // y >= minY                     ClipAlongDy(ref t0, ref t1, dy, p0y, minY, true);                     // y <= maxY                     ClipAlongDy(ref t0, ref t1, dy, p0y, maxY, false);                      if (t0 <= t1)                     {                         var A = new Pt(p0x + dx * t0, p0y + dy * t0);                         var B = new Pt(p0x + dx * t1, p0y + dy * t1);                          // Discard degenerate edges                         if (Distance2(A, B) > 1e-12)                             edges.Add(new Seg(A, B));                     }                 }             }              return edges;         }          static void ClipAlongDx(ref double t0, ref double t1, double dx, double p0x, double bound, bool keepGreaterEqual)         {             if (Math.Abs(dx) < 1e-12) // parallel to vertical clip             {                 // If p0x already outside, no intersection                 double x = p0x;                 if (keepGreaterEqual && x < bound - 1e-12) { t0 = 1; t1 = 0; }                 if (!keepGreaterEqual && x > bound + 1e-12) { t0 = 1; t1 = 0; }                 return;             }             double t = (bound - p0x) / dx;             if (keepGreaterEqual)             {                 if (t > t0) t0 = t;             }             else             {                 if (t < t1) t1 = t;             }         }          static void ClipAlongDy(ref double t0, ref double t1, double dy, double p0y, double bound, bool keepGreaterEqual)         {             if (Math.Abs(dy) < 1e-12)             {                 double y = p0y;                 if (keepGreaterEqual && y < bound - 1e-12) { t0 = 1; t1 = 0; }                 if (!keepGreaterEqual && y > bound + 1e-12) { t0 = 1; t1 = 0; }                 return;             }             double t = (bound - p0y) / dy;             if (keepGreaterEqual)             {                 if (t > t0) t0 = t;             }             else             {                 if (t < t1) t1 = t;             }         }          static double Distance2(Pt a, Pt b)         {             double dx = a.X - b.X, dy = a.Y - b.Y;             return dx * dx + dy * dy;         }     } } ```  Notes: - Complexity is O(n^3) in the worst case (for each pair i,j you loop over all other sites to impose half-plane constraints), suitable for modest point counts. - The method computes exact Voronoi edges by intersection of a pair’s perpendicular bisector with all site-based half-planes and the boundary rectangle. - No external libraries are required; it’s a self-contained approach.
8|36: Here’s a different, self-contained approach: compute an approximate Fortune-style Voronoi diagram by a distance transform on a grid within the boundary, then extract the boundary edges between neighboring grid cells owned by different sites. This clips naturally to a rectangular boundary and avoids implementing Delaunay or Fortune sweeps.  ```csharp using System; using System.Collections.Generic;  namespace VoronoiGridApprox {     struct Pt { public double X, Y; public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; } }      struct Segment { public Pt A, B; public Segment(Pt a, Pt b) { A = a; B = b; } }      public struct Rect { public double MinX, MinY, MaxX, MaxY; public Rect(double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)         { MinX = minX; MinY = minY; MaxX = maxX; MaxY = maxY; } }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             var boundary = new Rect(0, 0, 800, 600);              // Sample sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120),                 new Pt(260, 60),                 new Pt(340, 210),                 new Pt(480, 150),                 new Pt(640, 320),                 new Pt(720, 420),                 new Pt(200, 520)             };              // Grid resolution (cell size in world units)             int cell = 8; // smaller -> better accuracy, larger -> faster              var edges = BuildVoronoiGridApprox(sites, boundary, cell);              foreach (var s in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({s.A.X:0.0},{s.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({s.B.X:0.0},{s.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Grid-based approximate Voronoi clipped to the boundary         public static List<Segment> BuildVoronoiGridApprox(List<Pt> sites, Rect boundary, int cell)         {             int cols = (int)Math.Ceiling((boundary.MaxX - boundary.MinX) / cell);             int rows = (int)Math.Ceiling((boundary.MaxY - boundary.MinY) / cell);              // owner[i,j] = index of nearest site for grid cell centered at (i,j)             var owner = new int[cols, rows];             for (int i = 0; i < cols; i++)             {                 for (int j = 0; j < rows; j++)                 {                     double x = boundary.MinX + (i + 0.5) * cell;                     double y = boundary.MinY + (j + 0.5) * cell;                      int best = -1;                     double bestD = double.MaxValue;                     for (int s = 0; s < sites.Count; s++)                     {                         double dx = sites[s].X - x;                         double dy = sites[s].Y - y;                         double d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;                         if (d2 < bestD)                         {                             bestD = d2;                             best = s;                         }                     }                     owner[i, j] = best;                 }             }              var edges = new List<Segment>();              // Vertical edges between (i,j) and (i+1,j)             for (int i = 0; i < cols - 1; i++)             {                 for (int j = 0; j < rows; j++)                 {                     int a = owner[i, j];                     int b = owner[i + 1, j];                     if (a != b)                     {                         double x = boundary.MinX + (i + 1) * cell;                         double y0 = boundary.MinY + j * cell;                         double y1 = y0 + cell;                         edges.Add(new Segment(new Pt(x, y0), new Pt(x, y1)));                     }                 }             }              // Horizontal edges between (i,j) and (i,j+1)             for (int i = 0; i < cols; i++)             {                 for (int j = 0; j < rows - 1; j++)                 {                     int a = owner[i, j];                     int b = owner[i, j + 1];                     if (a != b)                     {                         double y = boundary.MinY + (j + 1) * cell;                         double x0 = boundary.MinX + i * cell;                         double x1 = x0 + cell;                         edges.Add(new Segment(new Pt(x0, y), new Pt(x1, y)));                     }                 }             }              // Edges are already clipped to the boundary by construction             return edges;         }     } } ```  Notes: - This is an approximate, grid-based method suitable for visualization and interactive use with modest point counts. - Adjust the cell size (smaller is more accurate but slower) to balance quality and performance. - It avoids external libraries and is simple to adapt to other boundaries.
9|36: Here's a fresh, self-contained approach: an explicit Jump Flooding Algorithm (JFA) to compute a close approximation of a 2D Voronoi diagram on a rectangular boundary, then extract and clip the edges to the boundary. This avoids implementing Fortune or Delaunay directly and yields a fast, simple solution.  ```csharp using System; using System.Collections.Generic;  namespace VoronoiJFA {     struct Pt { public double X, Y; public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; } }     struct Seg { public Pt A, B; public Seg(Pt a, Pt b) { A = a; B = b; } }     struct Rect { public double MinX, MinY, MaxX, MaxY; public Rect(double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)         { MinX = minX; MinY = minY; MaxX = maxX; MaxY = maxY; } }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             var boundary = new Rect(0, 0, 800, 600);              // Sample sites             var sites = new List<Pt>             {                 new Pt(100, 120),                 new Pt(260, 60),                 new Pt(340, 210),                 new Pt(480, 150),                 new Pt(640, 320),                 new Pt(720, 420),                 new Pt(200, 520)             };              // JFA parameters             int cellSize = 4; // grid cell size in world units (lower = better accuracy)             int w = (int)Math.Ceiling((boundary.MaxX - boundary.MinX) / cellSize);             int h = (int)Math.Ceiling((boundary.MaxY - boundary.MinY) / cellSize);              var edges = ComputeVoronoiJFA(sites, boundary, w, h, cellSize);              foreach (var e in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({e.A.X:0.0},{e.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({e.B.X:0.0},{e.B.Y:0.0})");         }          // Jump Flooding Algorithm to approximate Voronoi, then extract clipped edges         public static List<Seg> ComputeVoronoiJFA(List<Pt> sites, Rect boundary, int w, int h, int cellSize)         {             // 1) Create a grid that stores the nearest site index for each cell             int[,] owner = new int[w, h];             for (int i = 0; i < w; i++) for (int j = 0; j < h; j++) owner[i, j] = -1;              // Map sites to grid cells (rough placement)             for (int s = 0; s < sites.Count; s++)             {                 int gx = (int)Math.Clamp((sites[s].X - boundary.MinX) / cellSize, 0, w - 1);                 int gy = (int)Math.Clamp((sites[s].Y - boundary.MinY) / cellSize, 0, h - 1);                 owner[gx, gy] = s;             }              // Helper: distance from cell center to a site             double Dist2(int gx, int gy, int siteIndex)             {                 double x = boundary.MinX + (gx + 0.5) * cellSize;                 double y = boundary.MinY + (gy + 0.5) * cellSize;                 var p = sites[siteIndex];                 double dx = p.X - x, dy = p.Y - y;                 return dx * dx + dy * dy;             }              // 2) Jump Flooding: step is power of two, halving             int maxStep = 1;             while (maxStep < Math.Max(w, h)) maxStep <<= 1;             int step = maxStep;             while (step > 0)             {                 // Copy to avoid in-place ripple effects that could bias                 var next = new int[w, h];                 Array.Copy(owner, next, owner.Length);                  for (int x = 0; x < w; x++)                 {                     for (int y = 0; y < h; y++)                     {                         int cur = owner[x, y];                         double curD = cur >= 0 ? Dist2(x, y, cur) : double.MaxValue;                          // Examine 9 neighbors at distance 'step'                         for (int dx = -1; dx <= 1; dx++)                         {                             for (int dy = -1; dy <= 1; dy++)                             {                                 if (dx == 0 && dy == 0) continue;                                 int nx = x + dx * step;                                 int ny = y + dy * step;                                 if (nx < 0 || nx >= w || ny < 0 || ny >= h) continue;                                 int nk = owner[nx, ny];                                 if (nk < 0) continue;                                 double nd = Dist2(x, y, nk);                                 if (nd < curD)                                 {                                     next[x, y] = nk;                                     curD = nd;                                 }                             }                         }                     }                 }                  owner = next;                 step >>= 1;             }              // 3) Extract edges by checking adjacency between cells of different owners             var edges = new List<Seg>();              // Vertical edges between (i,j) and (i+1,j)             for (int i = 0; i < w - 1; i++)             {                 for (int j = 0; j < h; j++)                 {                     int a = owner[i, j];                     int b = owner[i + 1, j];                     if (a != b)                     {                         double x = boundary.MinX + (i + 1) * cellSize;                         double y0 = boundary.MinY + j * cellSize;                         double y1 = y0 + cellSize;                         edges.Add(new Seg(new Pt(x, y0), new Pt(x, y1)));                     }                 }             }              // Horizontal edges between (i,j) and (i,j+1)             for (int i = 0; i < w; i++)             {                 for (int j = 0; j < h - 1; j++)                 {                     int a = owner[i, j];                     int b = owner[i, j + 1];                     if (a != b)                     {                         double y = boundary.MinY + (j + 1) * cellSize;                         double x0 = boundary.MinX + i * cellSize;                         double x1 = x0 + cellSize;                         edges.Add(new Seg(new Pt(x0, y), new Pt(x1, y)));                     }                 }             }              // Edges are clipped to the boundary by construction             return edges;         }     } } ```  Notes: - This uses a CPU-friendly Jump Flooding Algorithm to quickly approximate a Voronoi diagram on a fixed grid. It’s not a perfect Fortune diagram but yields a fast, visually reasonable mesh clipped to the rectangle. - Adjust cellSize to trade accuracy vs. performance. Smaller values give finer edges but heavier memory and compute. - No external libraries are required; it’s a self-contained approach suitable for quick prototyping or visualization.
10|36: // Another approach: use NetTopologySuite's VoronoiDiagramBuilder to produce // the diagram clipped to a rectangular boundary, then extract edges.  using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using NetTopologySuite.Geometries; using NetTopologySuite.Algorithm.Voronoi;  namespace VoronoiNtsClippedDemo {     struct Pt { public double X, Y; public Pt(double x, double y) { X = x; Y = y; } }     struct Segment { public Pt A, B; public Segment(Pt a, Pt b) { A = a; B = b; } }      class Program     {         static void Main()         {             // Boundary rectangle             double minX = 0, minY = 0, maxX = 800, maxY = 600;             var boundaryEnv = new Envelope(minX, maxX, minY, maxY);              // Sample sites             var sites = new List<Coordinate>             {                 new Coordinate(100, 120),                 new Coordinate(260, 60),                 new Coordinate(340, 210),                 new Coordinate(480, 150),                 new Coordinate(640, 320),                 new Coordinate(720, 420),                 new Coordinate(200, 520)             };              var factory = new GeometryFactory();              // Build and clip Voronoi diagram to boundary             var builder = new VoronoiDiagramBuilder();             builder.SetSites(sites);             builder.ClipEnvelope = boundaryEnv;              var diagram = builder.GetDiagram(factory);              // Extract edges from clipped polygons             var edges = new List<Segment>();             var seen = new HashSet<string>();              foreach (var g in diagram.Geometries)             {                 if (g is Polygon poly)                 {                     var coords = poly.ExteriorRing.Coordinates;                     for (int i = 0; i < coords.Length - 1; i++)                     {                         var a = coords[i];                         var b = coords[i + 1];                         string key = MakeKey(a, b);                         if (!seen.Contains(key) && !seen.Contains(MakeKey(b, a)))                         {                             edges.Add(new Segment(new Pt(a.X, a.Y), new Pt(b.X, b.Y)));                             seen.Add(key);                         }                     }                 }             }              foreach (var e in edges)                 Console.WriteLine($"Edge: ({e.A.X:0.0},{e.A.Y:0.0}) -> ({e.B.X:0.0},{e.B.Y:0.0})");         }          static string MakeKey(Coordinate a, Coordinate b)         {             // undirected edge key with rounding             int ax = (int)Math.Round(a.X * 1000);             int ay = (int)Math.Round(a.Y * 1000);             int bx = (int)Math.Round(b.X * 1000);             int by = (int)Math.Round(b.Y * 1000);             if (ax < bx || (ax == bx && ay <= by))                 return $"{ax}:{ay}-{bx}:{by}";             else                 return $"{bx}:{by}-{ax}:{ay}";         }     } }

1|39: One plausible design is a standard 3-way (two-switch) circuit so two SPDT switches control a single light from opposite ends.  What you need: - 2 x SPDT (3-way) switches - 14/3 NM cable (between the two switches) — carries two travelers and ground - 14/2 NM cable from power source to Switch 1 - 14/2 NM cable from Switch 2 to the light - Ground wires, wire nuts, tape for re-identifying conductors  Wiring plan: - Power source hot (live) from the panel goes to the common terminal of Switch 1 (SW1 COM). - Two traveler wires run between the switches: connect traveler terminals on SW1 to traveler terminals on Switch 2 (SW2). Use the two insulated conductors in the 14/3 between the switches (commonly red and white; re-identify the white as hot). - The common terminal of Switch 2 (SW2 COM) connects to the hot lead going to the light. - The neutral from the power source is connected directly to the other lead of the light (do not switch the neutral). - Tie all grounds together (panel ground, both switches, and the light).  How it works: - The hot path to the lamp depends on the position of either switch. Flipping either switch opens/closes a path through one of the two traveler wires, allowing the circuit to complete to the lamp or break it, turning the light on or off from either end of the room.  Notes: - If the power source is routed differently (e.g., power to the light first), the wiring configuration changes; the above is the common arrangement with power to Switch 1 and the light fed from Switch 2. - Mark any white traveler conductor with tape to indicate it’s hot.
2|39: Alternative design: two momentary pushbuttons driving a latching relay (relay-based toggle)  What you need: - 1 x mains-rated latching relay (DPDT or two-coil bistable relay) capable of handling the lamp current - 2 x momentary pushbuttons (normally open), rated for mains - Suitable wiring and enclosure, plus line, neutral, and ground as required by code  Wiring concept (high level): - The lamp is powered through the normally-open contacts of the latching relay; its other side connects to neutral. - The hot supply from the panel goes to the common of a simple two-button control circuit that toggles the relay:   - Pressing Button A (or Button B) energizes the relay’s Set coil to switch the relay ON.   - Pressing the other button energizes the Reset coil to switch the relay OFF. - Because the relay is latching, either button can turn the light on or off from either end of the room. The two pushbuttons can be mounted at opposite ends and wired to the two coils (Set/Reset) with appropriate isolation and current-limiting provisions per the relay’s datasheet.  How it works: - When you press either pushbutton, the coil corresponding to that button is energized, causing the relay to change state and latch (either ON or OFF). The lamp follows the relay’s NO contact, so pressing either button toggles the light from either location.  Notes: - Ensure all components are rated for the local mains voltage and current, and follow local electrical codes. This approach uses a relay-based toggle instead of traditional 3-way switches, providing identical “two switches control one light from opposite ends” functionality in a different implementation. If unsure, consult a licensed electrician.

6|39: Alternative design: electronic toggle using a flip‑flop and a mains relay  Idea Two momentary pushbuttons at opposite ends of the room act as a single "toggle" input. Each press clocks a small logic circuit that toggles a relay, which in turn powers the lamp. This gives true two-location control without running a traditional 3‑way switch wiring.  What you need - 1 x mains-rated relay (or solid-state relay) capable of switching the lamp current - 1 x isolated 5 V DC power supply (mains to 5 V) - 1 x dual D-type flip-flop IC (e.g., 74HC74) or a similar toggle IC - 2 x momentary pushbuttons (normally open), mounted at opposite ends - 2 x debouncing components for each button (e.g., small RC networks; optionally a Schmitt-trigger input stage) - 1 x NPN transistor (e.g., 2N2222) to drive the relay coil - Flyback diode across the relay coil - Basic resistors, capacitors, and a suitable enclosure - Wiring, connectors, and safety-rated mounting hardware  Wiring concept (high level) - Lamp neutral goes directly to the power neutral. - Lamp hot goes through the relay contacts to the hot supply. - The relay coil is driven by the 5 V supply via the transistor; the transistor is controlled by the Q output of the flip-flop. - The two pushbuttons feed into the clock input of the flip-flop through simple debouncing networks. Pressing either button produces a clock edge, which toggles Q. - The D input of the flip-flop is tied to Q (D = Q), so each clock edge toggles the state (a classic toggle flip-flop arrangement). - The Q output drives the transistor, which energizes the relay coil to switch the lamp on or off. - Ensure the 5 V supply is isolated from the mains and that the relay coil circuit is isolated from the lamp circuit (as appropriate for the chosen relay).  How it works - Pressing either pushbutton creates a short clock edge. The flip-flop toggles its output with every press. - The relay follows the flip-flop output, turning the lamp on or off. Because the flip-flop retains state with power, the lamp stays in its last state until you press one of the buttons again.  Notes - Use a mains-rated relay or SSR appropriate for the lamp current. The 5 V logic circuitry must be isolated from the mains; a properly isolated supply and appropriate enclosures are essential. - Debounce each button to avoid multiple rapid toggles from a single press. - If you’re not comfortable working with mains electronics, consult a licensed electrician. This design provides two-location control via an electronic toggle rather than traditional mechanical 3-way wiring.

1|41: Sample Project Manager interview Q&A  - Question: Tell me about yourself and why you’re a good fit for a Project Manager role.   - Answer: I’ve spent the last eight years delivering IT and software projects across finance and operations. I started as a software engineer, moved into PM, and have led cross‑functional teams of 8–20 people. In my last role I steered a $2.5M CRM implementation across seven departments, delivering on time and 5% under budget, while cutting time-to-market by about 30%. I’m energized by turning unclear problems into actionable plans, communicating clearly with stakeholders, and continuously improving processes.  - Question: Describe a challenging project and how you delivered it.   - Answer: In a previous project, we had a critical dependency on an external vendor with a history of delays. I implemented a dual-track approach: (1) kept the vendor on schedule with weekly risk reviews and tight milestones, and (2) created a parallel internal workaround for the highest-risk features. I also established a formal change-control process to prevent scope creep. Result: we delivered the core system on time, with the workaround reducing outage risk by 40% and the project ending within 3% of the original budget.  - Question: How do you manage stakeholders and align expectations?   - Answer: I establish a stakeholder map early, define a RACI matrix, and set a clear communications plan with regular cadence (weekly status, monthly steering meeting). I translate technical progress into business terms, surface risks early, and document agreed decisions. This creates transparency and reduces last-minute surprises, keeping alignment even when priorities shift.  - Question: How do you handle changing requirements and scope creep?   - Answer: I use a formal change-control process: any new requirement is assessed for business value, impact on scope, timeline, and budget, and then prioritized in the backlog with input from key sponsors. I maintain a frozen baseline for delivery milestones and reserve a contingency buffer for high-priority changes. Regular backlog grooming and stakeholder reviews ensure the team isn’t pulled in conflicting directions.  - Question: What project management tools and metrics do you rely on?   - Answer: I use Jira for task and backlog management, Confluence for documentation, and dashboards in Power BI/Excel for reporting. Key metrics I track include burn-down/burn-up charts, schedule variance, cost variance, and risk exposure. I also track lead time and cycle time to identify bottlenecks and drive process improvements.  - Question: How do you motivate a team and handle conflicts?   - Answer: I foster psychological safety by encouraging open dialogue and recognizing both individual and team contributions. In conflicts, I facilitate a structured discussion to surface root causes, align on shared goals, and agree on concrete actions. I also ensure clear priorities, realistic commitments, and regular feedback loops so the team feels supported and accountable.  If you want, I can tailor this to a specific industry (software, construction, manufacturing) or to a particular methodology (Agile/Scrum, Waterfall, hybrid).

In my last role, I steered a cloud-based analytics platform migration for a regulated industry, delivering in 8 months with 12% under budget and a 25% improvement in user adoption thanks to user-centered planning and incremental releases.  - Question: Describe a challenging project and how you delivered it.   - Answer: We faced a tight deadline for a data consolidation initiative with a complex data governance model and multiple data owners. I implemented a dual-track approach: (1) a formal PMO-driven plan with fixed milestones and weekly risk reviews, and (2) a lightweight, collaborative data-steward workbook to parallelize data cleansing. I established a governance board to approve scope changes quickly and created MVP data sets to demonstrate progress early. Outcome: on-time delivery of the core data model, with data quality improving by 40% within the first quarter and a smooth handoff to operations.  - Question: How do you manage stakeholders and align expectations?   - Answer: I start with a stakeholder map segmented by influence and impact, create a clear RACI, and set a predictable governance cadence (biweekly touchpoints, monthly steering). I translate technical progress into business terms, surface risks early, and maintain an independent issue log with decisions and owners. This fosters transparency and helps navigate competing priorities without derailing the plan.  - Question: How do you handle changing requirements and scope creep?   - Answer: I use a formal change-control process tied to business value: every change is scoped, value-ranked, and assessed for impact on schedule and budget. I keep a frozen baseline for delivery milestones and maintain a contingency buffer for high-priority shifts. Regular backlog refinement and sponsor reviews ensure we prioritize the work that truly drives value while controlling scope.  - Question: What project management tools and metrics do you rely on?   - Answer: Tools: Jira for backlog and task tracking, Confluence for documentation, and Power BI for dashboards. Metrics: schedule variance, cost variance, earned value, risk exposure, and throughput metrics like lead time and cycle time. I also track team velocity and release burn-down to inform continuous improvement.  - Question: How do you motivate a team and handle conflicts?   - Answer: I cultivate psychological safety by inviting diverse perspectives and recognizing both individual and team contributions. When conflicts arise, I facilitate structured discussions to uncover root causes, align on shared goals, and agree on concrete actions with owners and deadlines. I also ensure clear priorities and realistic commitments, with regular feedback loops so the team stays engaged and accountable.  If you’d like, I can tailor this to a specific industry (software, construction, manufacturing) or to a particular methodology (Agile/Scrum, Waterfall, hybrid).

1|44: Here's a tiny, plausible example of a Godot 4 C++ extension (GDExtension) that adds a new node with a greet method. It shows a single class HelloNode that you can attach in a scene and call say_hello from GDScript or C++.  Files:  // hello_node.h #pragma once #include <godot_cpp/core/class_db.hpp> #include <godot_cpp/classes/node.hpp>  using namespace godot;  class HelloNode : public Node {     GDCLASS(HelloNode, Node); public:     static void _bind_methods();     String greet() const; };    // hello_node.cpp #include "hello_node.h"  void HelloNode::_bind_methods() {     ClassDB::bind_method(D_METHOD("greet"), &HelloNode::greet); }  String HelloNode::greet() const {     return "Hello from C++ plugin!"; }  Usage (one plausible approach):  - Compile this as a Godot 4 GDExtension library (build steps depend on your setup, typically using SCons/CMake with godot-cpp bindings). - Load the compiled library in Godot as a GDExtension module. - Create a new node of type HelloNode in a scene (Godot will expose the class due to _bind_methods). - In GDScript or C++, call:  var n = HelloNode.new() print(n.greet())  # prints: Hello from C++ plugin!  Notes:  - This is intentionally minimal: it only exposes a greet() method. You can add properties, signals, or additional methods by extending _bind_methods and the class.  - For a full plugin, you’d typically include a plugin manifest (e.g., a plugin config file) and build automation (SCons or CMake) to produce a shared library that Godot loads as a GDExtension.
